<p class="lead">
My central question is how a low-energy effective theory reveals whether it can arise
from a consistent theory of quantum gravity. In string compactifications, much of this
information is encoded in the geometry of moduli spaces and in the behaviour of the
theory near their boundaries.
</p>

## Research programme

<div class="research-grid">

::: {.research-card}
### Infinite-distance limits and emergent strings

Infinite-distance limits are regimes in which an effective theory develops an infinite
tower of light states. I study how these towers arise geometrically in Calabi–Yau
compactifications and whether the limiting theory is governed by a weakly coupled
critical string or by decompactification to a higher-dimensional theory.

A major goal is to connect the Hodge-theoretic classification of type II, III, and IV
degenerations to explicit geometric cycles, BPS states, effective strings, and their
higher-dimensional duality frames.
:::

::: {.research-card}
### Asymptotic Hodge theory

Periods of Calabi–Yau manifolds determine many physical couplings, but their exact form
is often inaccessible. Nilpotent-orbit and \(SL(2)\)-orbit techniques provide universal
control near singular boundaries.

I develop these mathematical results into calculational tools for moduli-space metrics,
gauge couplings, flux potentials, BPS masses, and the structure of multi-parameter
degenerations.
:::

::: {.research-card}
### Quantum obstructions in \(\mathcal{N}=1\) theories

A limit that appears consistent in a classical effective action need not survive quantum
corrections. In four-dimensional \(\mathcal{N}=1\) compactifications, different moduli
sectors generically fail to factorise at the quantum level.

My work studies how string-coupling and Kähler-sector corrections can obstruct pure
complex-structure limits, requiring correlated trajectories through the full field space.
:::

::: {.research-card}
### Finiteness and the flux landscape

String compactifications admit large families of flux vacua. A fundamental problem is
to understand which sets of vacua are finite, how complicated they can be, and how they
accumulate near boundaries of moduli space.

I use asymptotic Hodge theory together with ideas from tame and o-minimal geometry to
formulate and investigate precise finiteness and counting questions.
:::

</div>

## Current directions

### Geodesics and asymptotic field-space geometry

The Swampland Distance Conjecture is naturally formulated along geodesic trajectories,
yet the metrics of general Calabi–Yau moduli spaces are not locally symmetric and can
contain asymptotically degenerate directions. I am investigating how essential instanton
corrections resolve these directions and how the resulting geodesics determine the
physical rate at which towers become light.

### Hodge loci, worldsheet CFT, and generalized symmetry

Special loci in complex-structure moduli space can support additional arithmetic or
geometric structure. I am exploring how such Hodge loci are represented in the
worldsheet conformal field theory and whether they are characterised by additional
topological defect lines and generalized symmetries.

### Singular Calabi–Yau spaces and quantum gravity

Compact singular Calabi–Yau geometries offer a controlled setting in which gauge,
gravitational, and strongly coupled sectors interact. I am interested in extracting
general quantum-gravity constraints directly from their degeneration and resolution
structure.

## Methodological perspective

My research combines several layers that are often treated separately:

- **Effective field theory:** moduli-space metrics, BPS objects, towers of states, and
  quantum corrections.
- **Algebraic and differential geometry:** Calabi–Yau degenerations, fibrations,
  singularities, and special Lagrangian cycles.
- **Hodge theory:** period maps, limiting mixed Hodge structures, and asymptotic
  \(SL(2)\)-data.
- **Quantum-gravity constraints:** distance, emergence, finiteness, and consistency
  conditions.

<div class="info-box">
The unifying aim is not only to classify possible asymptotic behaviours, but to identify
the microscopic physics that realises them and the quantum effects that rule out
apparently consistent classical limits.
</div>
